records.cool_rest_note: Goes dormant in fall, with dormancy continuing until spring; in cold climates dead leaf tissue should be trimmed back in winter as pitchers die, but only the dead tissue, with foliage otherwise left until just before spring flowering.
records.name_note: RHS and MoBot both designate 'yellow pitcher plant' as this species' primary common name: RHS's dedicated Sarracenia flava page renders 'yellow pitcher plant' as the subtitle beneath its 'RHS Plant Profile' label and lists 'biscuits, huntsman's horn, trumpets, water cup, yellow sidesaddle flower, yellow trumpets' separately under 'Other common names'; MoBot's page carries a single line reading 'Common Name: yellow pitcher plant'. NC State's Plant Toolbox canonical page is headed 'Sarracenia flava' and lists five names alphabetically under 'Common Name(s):' (Giant Red Tube, Huntsman Horn, Trumpets, Yellow Pitcher Plant, Yellow Trumpet). The name is not unique to this species: NC State's page carries a structured cross-reference 'Other plants called Yellow Pitcher Plant: Sarracenia alata', and NC State's Sarracenia alata page also lists 'Yellow Pitcher Plant' among that species' common names. Distinct from Sarracenia purpurea (Purple Pitcher Plant) already in this catalog.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the only admissible-source toxicity statement found is NC State's Edibility field — "The root and leaves are sometimes used in herbal remedies but can be toxic and sometimes fatal in high quantities or if misused." — which is human-scoped (herbal-remedy misuse) and names no animal at all, so per the wholly-unscoped rule it cannot support toxic_to_pets=true or false. No admissible source discusses cat or dog toxicity for this species.

soil_base left null: none of the allowed enum tokens (standard_potting, chunky_aroid, cactus_succulent, ericaceous, orchid_bark, african_violet, semi_hydro, garden_bed) accurately represents the peat/sand/perlite/sphagnum carnivorous-bog mix described by NC State and MoBot, so no value was forced.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field is the open-ended "Acid (<6.0)" band (no floor stated per the rules) and RHS's pH field is only the qualitative "Acid or Neutral" with no numeric band, so no admissible source supplies a specific pH ceiling or floor.

chill_damage_f left null: no admissible source states a numeric damage-onset temperature. RHS's species page renders only the chip 'H3'; the site-wide ratings legend reads "H3: hardy in coastal and relatively mild parts of the UK (-5 to 1)" (the unit appears separately in the modal preamble, 'Minimum temperature ranges (in degrees C) are shown in brackets'). That is a hardiness/survival rating and site-wide legend text, not a damage-onset figure, so it was not used per the rules.
day/night temperature fields left null: no admissible source gives explicit daytime or nighttime temperature ranges for this species.
humidity_need and humidity_pct fields left null: no admissible source states a humidity requirement or percentage for Sarracenia flava.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max left null: no admissible source gives footcandle values or species-specific prose stating a maximum number of direct-sun hours; the only hour figure is the parenthetical inside NC State's standardized Light category label ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'), which renders as this page's Light value but is a site-wide category definition rather than species-specific prose, so it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max per the rules.

fertilize_* fields left null: sources actively advise against fertilizing this species rather than giving a schedule — NC State states "This plant does not like fertilizers... fertilizers can burn the plant," and MoBot's Problems section states "Do not fertilize plantings." No admissible source gives an interval, active months, or dilution strength, and per instructions no fertilize_* value was inferred from general carnivorous-plant lore.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, and water_dry_down_target left null: no admissible source frames watering for this species as a dry-down/check-depth/day-interval regimen — instead sources direct that soil be kept constantly, consistently moist/wet and never allowed to dry out, which is captured in water_regime=keep_moist instead.

soil_drainage=moisture_retentive is drawn from NC State ("constantly damp, but not watery, bog garden") and MoBot ("constantly damp but not watery. Soils must never dry out"), both explicit species-specific statements requesting consistently wet/boggy conditions. This is disclosed as a partial conflict with RHS's structured Moisture field for this same species page, which reads "Moist but well-drained or Poorly-drained" — a milder framing that, per the rules, would on its own read closer to the moderate/moisture_retentive boundary rather than clearly moisture_retentive; RHS's inclusion of "Poorly-drained" as an alternative option keeps it from flatly contradicting the wetter reading.

is_houseplant=false is drawn from NC State and MoBot's explicit statements that the species does not grow well as a houseplant (both citing the need for a genuine cold winter dormancy). Two conflicts are disclosed. RHS's Sarracenia flava page carries a 'Houseplants' category badge alongside 'Bogs' and 'Conservatory Greenhouse' near the top of the page, without further species-specific houseplant-suitability prose. And MoBot's own Uses section reads: "Bog garden is best. Also may be grown in containers, greenhouses or as an indoor houseplant. Perhaps too tall for terraria. Growth in containers as an indoor plant can be difficult because of the need for growing season sun and winter dormancy." -- so MoBot both allows indoor growing and says the plants 'simply do not grow well as houseplants'. The value stands because both sources' explicit suitability verdicts are negative and both tie it to the cold-dormancy requirement; this catalog's Purple Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia purpurea) landed true on the same MoBot wording plus an RHS growing guide, which this species lacks.

RHS's Cultivation paragraph ("Grow under glass, keep moist in full light... Most Sarracenias can be grown outside in milder parts of the country...") was treated as genus-level boilerplate per the scope-discipline rule (it explicitly generalizes to "Most Sarracenias") and was not used to support any field. Only RHS's page-specific structured fields (Position, Soil Types, Moisture, pH, Hardiness, Name Status) were considered admissible, and of those only Position and Name Status were actually used: Hardiness was rejected as a survival rating and Soil Types ('Loam, Sand') was left unused because soil_base stayed null.

Wild-harvest / protection statement, NC State's exact words: "Some pitcher plants are on the endangered species list while others are on the threatened list. These plants are threatened by habitat loss, development, and over-collection. Never harvest these plants from the wild. They are best purchased from a reputable carnivorous plant nursery."

NC State citations were moved at landing from the slug-parameterized view /plants/sarracenia-flava/common-name/yellow-pitcher-plant/ to the canonical /plants/sarracenia-flava/ page, whose H1 is the binomial; the one citation kept on the view is NC State's 'Other plants called Yellow Pitcher Plant: Sarracenia alata' cross-reference, which renders only there.

is_edible left null: none of the readable pages (NC State species page, NC State common-name page, RHS) mention edibility, toxicity, poisoning, or any 'Problem for' text for Sarracenia flava. Checked all three for 'Edible', 'Poison', 'Toxic', 'Problem for' with zero hits on each.

https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/sarracenia-alata/ is a different species (Sarracenia alata, a genus-sibling, not S. flava) and per the task rules a genus/sibling page is not used as a size or edibility substitute for this species' record; it was read only to confirm it has no size 'Dimensions' block for flava and adds nothing beyond corroborating pollinator attraction (Attracts: Bees, Pollinators) for the genus.

records.cool_rest_note: NC State describes a winter dormancy period: an indoor-grown plant sits in a small pot in a tray of distilled or rainwater during growth, and the plant must be allowed to go dormant in winter.
records.name_note: Admissible dedicated single-species pages split on the primary common name. RHS's page renders 'round-leaved sundew' as the lead common name in the heading block beneath the H1 botanical name, and lists 'common sundew' only inside its separate 'Other common names' field alongside eight other alternate names (dew plant, eyebright, gwlithlys, lustwort, moor-grass, red rot, rosa solis, youthwort). NC State's page carries a structured Common Name(s) field with exactly two entries, 'Common Sundew' listed first and 'Roundleaf Sundew' second; its rendered H1 is the botanical name alone and carries no common names. Because both sources maintain dedicated single-species pages but disagree on which name leads, common_name here follows RHS's rendered lead name; the app's naming may reasonably split between 'Round-leaved Sundew' and 'Common Sundew' depending on which source is followed. Distinct from Drosera capensis (Cape Sundew) already in this catalog.
unknowns: No admissible source states any toxicity information for this species with respect to cats or dogs (or any animal); toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than inferred.

No admissible source gives a numeric chill-damage onset temperature for this species; RHS's H5 hardiness rating is a survival/hardiness rating (per the rules) and was not used to derive chill_damage_f.
No admissible source gives day or night ambient temperature ranges for this species; left null.

No admissible source gives a humidity percentage or a humidity-need level (low/average/high) for this species; left null despite the plant's known bog habitat, since that would be an inference from general plant knowledge rather than sourced content.

No admissible source gives a foot-candle light figure for this species. The only hour figure is the parenthetical inside NC State's standardized Light category labels ('Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'), which render as this page's Light values but are site-wide category definitions rather than species-specific prose, so direct_sun_hours_max is left null.

soil_base is left null because the enum carries no sand or carnivorous-mix token: RHS's dedicated species page carries a structured 'Soil Types' value of 'Sand' (repeated as the soil value in its Growing Conditions block), and the allowed tokens (standard_potting, chunky_aroid, cactus_succulent, ericaceous, orchid_bark, african_violet, semi_hydro, garden_bed) include nothing that represents a sand or peat-substitute/sand carnivorous mix. RHS's Cultivation text ('equal parts fertiliser-free peat substitute and sand') is the 'Under glass grow in...' cultivation prose the scope-discipline rule excludes, so it was not used for any field; NC State's 'nutrient-free medium' is likewise not an enum token.

soil_ph_min/max are left null: NC State's Soil pH field is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band, which the rules say cannot set a ceiling or floor, and RHS's Soil pH field is a bare 'Acid' tag with no numeric value given on the page.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, and water_dormant_days_est are left null: no admissible source frames watering in terms of a dry-down target, a check depth, or a day-count interval for this species; sources instead describe continuous moisture with reduced watering in winter dormancy.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null: NC State explicitly instructs not to fertilize this carnivorous species at all ('Do not fertilize the plant; it will get all the nutrients it needs from the insects it traps'), so no interval or strength applies.

plantfinder.mobot.org, hgic.clemson.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu did not return a dedicated single-species page for Drosera rotundifolia in search; only NC State and RHS provided admissible dedicated-page content for this species.

RHS's Cultivation paragraph ('Under glass grow in a mix of equal parts fertiliser-free peat substitute and sand... The compost should be kept continually moist to wet during the growing season... During the winter, plants enter a period of dormancy so keep just moist during the winter and do not stand the plants in water.') was ruled 'Under glass grow in...' cultivation prose under the scope-discipline rule and, for consistency, was not used for cool_rest_note or water_regime either (the research record had cited it for both while excluding it for soil_base); both values rest on NC State's species text. RHS's winter instruction is disclosed here as an unused corroboration of the dormancy period.

records.name_note: NC State Extension's Plant Toolbox page for this species (the only admissible dedicated single-species page located) renders a Common Name(s) list whose first entry is "Moccasin-flower," followed by "Pink Lady Slipper"; the page's own Description prose uses "Pink lady slipper." The plant is also very widely known outside admissible sources as "Pink Lady's Slipper," but no other admissible-domain dedicated page was located to weigh in on which name leads.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox scopes its poison entry to "Poisonous to Humans" (not cats or dogs): Poison Severity is rated Medium, the listed symptom is "Skin irritation after contact," the toxic principle is Unidentified, the plant Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes, and the affected Poison Part is the Leaves. No cat- or dog-specific toxicity tag (e.g., a Problem-for-Cats/Dogs field) appears on the page. NC State also tags the species '#poisonous', lists 'Poisonous' among its four Plant Type values (Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant, Poisonous, Wildflower), and shows a page-level banner reading 'This plant has medium severity poison characteristics.' Separately, under Uses (Ethnobotany) the same page states 'In the past, the root was used as a remedy for nervousness, tooth pain, and muscle spasms.' -- a historical medicinal note, not an edibility endorsement; the poison entry covers leaves and skin contact only.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's only poison entry for this species is explicitly headed 'Poisonous to Humans' with a contact-dermatitis warning to skin; no cat- or dog-specific toxicity tag (e.g. Problem for Cats/Dogs) appears anywhere on the page, so there is no cat/dog-scoped evidence to support true or false.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field for this species is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band, which the schema rules say sets no floor or ceiling. No other admissible-domain source with a dedicated page for this species (to cross-check via an RHS-style pH field) was located.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figure on the page is the parenthetical '(Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' that NC State appends to its Partial Shade light category on every plant page. The tag selection is species-specific and was used for outdoor_sun_exposure, but the hour range inside it is site-wide legend text, so no hour figure was taken from it.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis left null: NC State gives only a structured Soil Drainage tag set (Good Drainage / Moist / Occasionally Dry), not a watering statement or a structured moisture field; this is also an in-ground woodland perennial rather than a plant framed on a watering schedule.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength were all left null because no admissible source states them for this species.

Source coverage: of the admissible domains, only plants.ces.ncsu.edu was found to carry a dedicated single-species page for Cypripedium acaule. hgic.clemson.edu, plantfinder.mobot.org / www.missouribotanicalgarden.org, edis.ifas.ufl.edu / ask.ifas.ufl.edu, www.rhs.org.uk, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu did not yield a locatable dedicated page for this species during this research, so no cross-source disagreement could be checked or disclosed beyond the single-source data reported here.

Mycorrhiza requirement (NC State, exact statement): "The seeds require the presence of a specific Rhizoctonia fungus to germinate and grow. As the plant matures the relationship becomes symbiotic with the fungus."

Do-not-dig / transplant warning (NC State, exact statement, kept verbatim because this is a protected wild orchid in several states): "They are difficult to transplant and grow and are best left to their native habitat which is dry to mesic, acidic forests and woodlands, often under pines, other conifers, and/or oak trees." No admissible source states a legal harvest/protection status for the species, so none is recorded.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in left null: the NC State page has no 'Dimensions' block and no whole-plant 'Height'/'Width' fields for this species; it gives only Leaf Length (3-6 inches) and Leaf Width (1-3 inches), which describe individual leaves, not overall plant stature or spread, so they were not used.

is_edible left null: the page has no 'Edible' field and makes no statement that any part of the plant is or is not eaten. It does mark the plant Poisonous (medium severity), with Poison Part: Leaves, Poison Symptoms: Skin irritation after contact, Poison Toxic Principle: Unidentified, and Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes -- flagged here for decision purposes even though is_edible was not set true.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's only hour figure appears inside the boilerplate category definition attached to its Light value ('Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)'), which is a site-wide tag definition rather than a species-specific measurement; Clemson's habitat prose gives no hour figure.

records.name_note: NC State's Plant Toolbox page (the only dedicated single-species page found in the admissible domain set) opens its Description with the name 'Orange fringe orchid' and lists five common names in alphabetical order -- Bobwhite's-mocassin, Orange Fringed Orchid, Orange Plume, Owl's Head, Yellow Fringed Orchid -- ranking none of them (this order also matches the page-title parenthetical, which is likewise alphabetical). A Clemson HGIC weekly photo roundup ('September Week 1 Plants', Sep 3, 2018) captions its photo of the species 'Yellow Fringed Orchid', misspelling the genus as 'Paltanthera'. The species has also been classified under the synonyms Blephariglotis ciliaris and Habenaria ciliaris per NC State's 'Previously known as' field.
unknowns: No RHS page exists for Platanthera ciliaris — only Platanthera bifolia, Platanthera chlorantha, and the genus-level Platanthera page were found — so RHS could not be used to check scientific_name_accepted, a soil pH ceiling, a hardiness rating, or any other field.

No admissible source (NC State, Clemson HGIC, or any other domain in the allowed list) discusses toxicity to cats or dogs, or to any animal, for this species, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null.

is_houseplant set false at landing: NC State's material treats it purely as an outdoor wetland/meadow perennial (Plant Type Native Plant / Perennial / Wildflower, USDA zones 8a-10b, 'Plant in a native meadow, bog, or pollinator garden.'); its Landscape Location list includes 'Container', an outdoor container use, and no admissible source frames it as a houseplant.

No admissible source gives a numeric chill-damage onset temperature or day/night degree ranges for this species; the only temperature-adjacent figure found is NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone rating (8a, 8b, 9a, 9b, 10a, 10b), which per the task rules is a zone/survival rating, not a damage-onset temperature, so it was not used to populate any temperature field.
